title: LG ELECTRONICS SHOWCASES INNOVATION AND GROWTH STRATEGY FOR ASIA AT LG INNOFEST 2026 APAC
summary: LG Electronics proudly showcased its latest innovations and region-specific solutions at LG InnoFest 2026 APAC, held in Busan from April 7–10. The showcase reaffirmed LG’s vision of creating smarter, more convenient, and more sustainable homes for the future.

title: Following enactment of Inland Revenue Bill: TIN to become mandatory for many services
summary: By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Following the enactment of the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Bill, which has already been gazetted, a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) certificate will become mandatory for a range of services. Accordingly, individuals will be required to present a TIN certificate when opening an account at any financial institution, obtaining approval for a building plan, registering a motor vehicle or renewing a vehicle licence, registering land or land ownership, registering a business, transferring shares of a company incorporated in Sri Lanka by a transferee, and obtaining credit cards. The new requirement is expected to come into effect from April.

title: GL urges Govt to address Middle East fallout
summary: By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Former Foreign Minister Prof. G.L. Peiris has written to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, warning that the ongoing crisis in the Middle East could have serious and immediate repercussions for Sri Lanka. Writing on behalf of concerned citizens, Prof. Peiris stressed the need for the Government to promptly communicate its position to both the public and the international community. The letter further noted that the crisis affects Sri Lanka in at least four key areas. First, escalating global oil prices are expected to drive up local fuel costs, significantly increasing the cost of living and aggravating the economic hardships already faced by the public. Second, export revenues, particularly from commodities such as tea, may decline due to restricted access to key markets affected by active military conflicts in the region. Third, the tourism and hotel sector is already experiencing considerable cancellations from prospective tourists from Europe, North America, and the Gulf, who face difficulties related to air travel across the affected regions. Fourth, the situation threatens the viability of remittances from Sri Lankan workers throughout the Gulf and wider areas, which are a critical source of foreign income for the country. Prof. Peiris stressed that citizens are prepared to assist the Government in addressing these multifaceted challenges and are actively discussing practical measures to mitigate the crisis’s effects. A public briefing is planned in the near future to share these discussions and proposals. He also urged the Government to release basic information on its approach to the crisis. This, he said, would allow the public to participate in an informed manner and help ensure transparency in navigating these troubling developments.

title: SJB condemns recent attack on Iran – Sajith
summary: By Sandasen Marasinghe Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa, yesterday (3), revealing the stance of the Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB), condemned the recent attack on Iran and called on the Sri Lankan Government to issue a similar statement. He added that Parliament should not be divided on this matter and should maintain a unified stance on the attack against a sovereign nation. He also condemned the retaliatory attacks targeting the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain. Addressing Parliament following President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, Opposition Leader Premadasa said the Government should not be reluctant to condemn the attack, as it constitutes a clear violation of international law, including Articles 2(4) and 2(7) of the United Nations Charter. He added that another nation could respond under the provisions of Article 51, which allows for self-defence. “We should not be divided as a Parliament on this matter and should maintain the same stance,” the Opposition Leader said. He further proposed that the entire House should condemn the attack as an assault on a sovereign nation. He added that it would be positive if the Government issued a statement condemning it, as the Government need not fear doing so. summary: By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Minister of Ports and Civil Aviation Anura Karunathilaka stated that the civil aviation industry has not yet returned to normalcy following the escalation of tensions in the Middle East, and that 205 flights were cancelled yesterday (3) alone, of which 107 were arrivals, and 98 were departures from BIA. title: Despite Middle East conflict: President assures no fuel shortage
summary: By Sandasen Marasinghe President Anura Kumara Dissanayake assured Parliament yesterday (3) that the country would not face a fuel shortage despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. He said that the country had a stock of fuel sufficient for 33 days as of yesterday, and with the arrival of a shipment on 7 March, it would increase to 40 days. He added that another four fuel ships are scheduled to arrive by 28 March. He confirmed that those ships are already loaded, the supply is confirmed, and with the arrival of these stocks, the country would not face any fuel shortage, given the existing conflict situation in the Middle East. He also said that Sri Lanka expects the parties involved in the conflict to choose the path of peace, as there are no victors in war. He further noted that such a conflict would affect the global economy, including Sri Lanka’s. The President added that the country has a stock of diesel sufficient for the next 33 days and petrol for the next 27 days. He stated that a fuel ship carrying 35,000 MT of petrol is expected to arrive in Sri Lanka on 7 or 8 March. A ship containing fuel from RM Parks is expected on 14 March, from SINOPEC on 17 March, from Indian Oil Company (IOC) on 21 March, and from Ceylon Petroleum Corporation on 28 March. title: Turning the page, continuing the journey
summary: Dear readers, Today marks the publication of the final daily print edition ofCeylon Today. This is not a moment we approach lightly. For little over 14 years, the daily edition has been part of your mornings – folded into briefcases, shared across office desks, read over tea, and debated in homes across the country. To have been welcomed into your daily lives has been both a privilege and a profound responsibility. The media landscape, in Sri Lanka and across the world, has changed in ways few could have fully anticipated. Technology evolves at an unrelenting pace, reader habits continue to shift, and the economics of print journalism grow ever more complex. After careful reflection, we have taken the difficult decision to cease publication of our daily print edition. Let us assure you: this is not a farewell to journalism, nor a retreat from our principles. Our commitment to accuracy, accountability, and ethical reporting remains unwavering. We will continue to serve the public interest with the same editorial independence and rigour that have defined us since our inception. Importantly, our Sunday edition will continue with renewed purpose. We look forward to bringing you a stronger, richer, and more thoughtfulCeylon Todayeach week: one that offers deeper analysis, broader perspectives, and carefully considered reporting on the issues that matter most. Transitions inevitably carry a note of nostalgia, but they also carry opportunity. As we turn this page, we do so with gratitude for your loyalty and with determination to evolve in ways that better serve you in the years ahead. Thank you for reading us, challenging us, and standing with us. We hope you will continue this journey with us every Sunday, and across our digital platforms, as we strive to deliver journalism worthy of your trust.

title: Amid Middle East, Red Sea disruptions: Colombo Free Zone offers safe cargo routing
summary: By Sulochana Ramiah Mohan Amid the ongoing instability in the Middle East and the Red Sea region, Colombo’s Free Zone operations have been positioned as a secure alternative routing solution for global cargo movements. With shipping lines and airlines facing operational disruptions and heightened security risks in affected zones, logistics operators in Colombo are offering contingency routing options to ensure continuity of trade and delivery commitments. The Colombo Free Zone is facilitating multiple routing combinations, including sea-to-sea (SEA/SEA), sea-to-air (SEA to AIR), air-to-sea (AIR to SEA), and air-to-air (AIR/AIR) transfers. The scope of services includes cross-stuffing, palletising, re-documentation, short-term storage, and onward booking — all conducted under Free Zone status, ensuring there is no duty impact on cargo in transit. Industry sources said the alternative routing mechanism enables shippers to bypass high-risk maritime and air corridors while effectively managing transit delays caused by the regional crisis. Logistics stakeholders noted that the initiative aims to provide immediate, flexible solutions for shipments requiring contingency arrangements, positioning Colombo as a reliable transshipment and redistribution hub during the ongoing geopolitical uncertainty.

title: How to Lead Without a Title: Influencing From Within
summary: By Prasanna Perera Leadership is often mistakenly associated with titles, corner offices, or positions of authority. However, in today’s dynamic work environments, true leadership exceeds these traditional markers. It lies in the ability to inspire, influence, and drive meaningful change, regardless of one’s official position within an organisation. The real challenge is to lead effectively without formal authority and to harness influence from within the system. This form of leadership cultivates collaboration, fosters innovation, and empowers individuals to reach their full potential. When positioned without a high-ranking title, you can leverage unconventional strategies to undermine traditional hierarchies. By questioning assumptions and proposing alternative solutions, you can challenge thestatus quo. This approach may unsettle those in leadership, prompting them to engage with your ideas. Undermining need not be obvious; subtle tactics like reshaping discussions and offering well-researched insights can position you as a thought leader over time. title: Compliant but Unacceptable: Lessons for Colombo from Sydney and London About Built Form and Public Amenity
summary: BY DR SARATH MATARAARACHCHI As outlined in previous columns, over the past two to three decades, entrepreneurial urbanism has swept across the globe with remarkable momentum, transforming cities and creating urban environments of unprecedented scale and ambition. This has occurred as Government coffers diminished to meet infrastructure demands and as modern society became more sophisticated through technological advances and rising aspirations. There was a strong incentive for private capital to invest in urban development, since cities are increasingly regarded as engines of growth, centres of power and prosperity. Supported by vast pools of capital and strong institutions, this trend has delivered iconic buildings, transformative infrastructure, and carefully curated urban landscapes that project power, prosperity, and international relevance, often serving political elites, corporate interests, and international capital, all within broadly predictable planning frameworks. In much of the Global South, however, what has emerged is a diluted and distorted version of this model, best described as pseudo-entrepreneurial urbanism. title: Forty years on, ‘honour’ still tries to silence women
summary: By Azra Syed Forty years ago, when I asked for my right to study, my family did not beat or kill me. Instead, they married me to the Quran — a symbolic punishment meant to end education without bloodshed. I was just 16 and continued to resist. My parents disowned me and sent me to live with my elder sister, who already had two young daughters and more responsibility than she could afford. They did not kill me. But they tried to kill my passion for education. That, too, is how ‘honour’ works. It does not always arrive with knives or ropes. Sometimes it comes quietly — through banishment, emotional exile, and the calculated narrowing of a woman’s future. Survival is permitted; ambition is not. And it is important to say this clearly. It was not culture, religion, or society that forced my parents’ hand, that shaped the fate of a Banaz Mahmod, or that authorised the sexual violence inflicted on a Mukhtar Mai. It was, and remains, a system. A system that encourages misogynistic and patriarchal societies by promoting a well-established and carefully managed propaganda: One that teaches families that control is duty, that punishment is protection, and that a woman’s autonomy is a threat to collective order. title: Sri Lanka’s Path to Strategic Sovereignty
summary: Sri Lanka’s future will be shaped not only by what the world does to us, but by how clearly we define and defend our own interests. In an era when every nation is effectively ‘for itself’, strategic sovereignty can no longer be an abstract slogan for Sri Lanka; it must become a deliberate national project. What strategic sovereignty means for a small State For a small state, strategic sovereignty is less about isolation and more about the capacity to make and implement independent choices in the shadow of larger powers. It is the ability to pursue national interests without becoming structurally dependent—economically, militarily, or technologically—on any single external actor. For Sri Lanka, this is complicated by geography and history. Sitting astride key Indian Ocean sea lanes, the island has long attracted interest from major powers, turning location into both an asset and a vulnerability. Small States typically balance two imperatives: influence and autonomy. They seek enough relevance in regional and global affairs to secure support and investment, while preserving the freedom to say “no” when core interests are threatened. This is the essential tension Sri Lanka must manage as India, China, the United States and others compete across the IndoPacific. Sri Lanka’s current strategic posture In recent years, Sri Lanka has attempted its own blend of nonalignment, hedging and strategic autonomy. Policy has been framed around “friendship towards all, enmity towards none”, with governments seeking economic assistance and security partnerships from multiple directions at once. Colombo has deepened engagement with India, including highlevel visits and economic cooperation, while simultaneously maintaining extensive Chinese involvement in infrastructure and debt restructuring. title: The Ripple Effect of Workplace Microaggressions
summary: By Prasanna Perera Workplace microaggressions are subtle yet damaging forces that shape professional environments in overlooked ways. Unlike overt discrimination or severe harassment, these persistent acts of exclusion, bias and arrogance erode confidence and hinder careers. Examples include a raised eyebrow at a junior employee’s suggestion, comments about a colleague of colour being “surprisingly well-spoken,” or jokes about a working mother’s dual responsibilities. While companies tout diversity and inclusion, the true measure of a workplace culture lies in the unspoken messages conveyed through everyday interactions, which can create invisible barriers for those affected. The deceptive nature of microaggressions –Microaggressions in the workplace act as a subtle yet sinister force, gradually undermining morale, motivation, and mental well-being. Unlike overt acts of discrimination, these seemingly minor slights are often overlooked or dismissed, allowing their detrimental effects to accumulate over time. You may not immediately recognise the harm they inflict on your confidence and career advancement, but eventually, you could grapple with self-doubt, questioning your worth in an environment that should uplift you. Acknowledging these issues is essential to advocate for a more inclusive and supportive workplace culture. The gaslighting cycle –The underhanded nature of microaggressions often leads to their invalidation. When you express discomfort about subtle slights, you may encounter responses that make you question your own experiences, causing you to feel irrational about your feelings. Over time, this can lead to internalising the belief that your concerns are trivial, resulting in silence and suffering. This dynamic not only protects the aggressors but also fosters a toxic culture where you feel powerless to address inappropriate behaviour. title: Robust Domestic Consumption Is China’s New Economic Engine
summary: By Dr. Imran Khalid In the world of international economics, there are moments that serve as a testament to the sheer scale and potential of a nation’s internal engine. For China, that moment is the Spring Festival – the largest annual human migration on the planet. This year, the “Year of the Horse” has delivered far more than a seasonal surge in travel. It has provided a definitive look at a world power successfully navigating the most significant pivot in modern history: the transition to a high-quality, consumption-driven economy. If you look at the data flowing out of Beijing, the numbers are, by any measure, breathtaking. We are witnessing a record-breaking holiday period that has effectively redefined the Chinese consumer’s role in the global market. Official reports indicate that nearly 9.5 billion cross-regional trips will be completed by the end of this travel rush. To put that in perspective, that is the equivalent of the entire global population moving across a continent and back again. But the real story is not just the volume of people; it is the unprecedented flow of capital. Data from the Ministry of Commerce shows that during this extended nine-day break, average daily sales for major retail and dining enterprises rose by 8.6 per cent compared to last year. In an era where many developed economies are searching for growth, these figures represent a massive, self-sustaining pulse of economic energy. What makes the 2026 Spring Festival a true turning point is the fundamental evolution in what the Chinese public is choosing to buy. title: Rumesh Shines, Secures Second in Maiden Diamond League
summary: Sri Lanka’s javelin sensation Rumesh Tharanga impressed on his Diamond League debut in Rabat , clinching second place with a throw of 85.97m on his very first attempt , his best effort of the night. Twice world champion Grenada’s Anderson Peters won the event with 86.08m, while former Olympic and World champion Keshorn Walcott of Trinidad and Tobago secured third with 82.52m. Rumesh’s performance was particularly notable as he outpaced a world-class field of 90m-plus throwers, including Germany’s Thomas Röhler and Kenya’s Julius Yego, who finished fourth and fifth respectively.

title: Tharushi Abhisheka Strikes Gold at Asian Junior Athletics Championship
summary: Middle-distance runner Tharushi Abhisheka opened Sri Lanka’s medal account at the Asian Junior (U20) Athletics Championship in Hong Kong, winning the Gold Medal in the Women’s 1500m. The 18-year-old clocked 4:31.41 to outpace Iran’s Maryam Baluoutaki and South Korea’s Song Dawson, who finished second and third respectively. Nicknamed“Podi Tharushi”on the local track—after Olympian Tharushi Karunarathne—Abhisheka competes in both the 800m and 1500m events under the guidance of coach Buddhika Nuwan. She received her early education at Gampola Wickramabahu MMV before moving to Lyceum International School, Wattala.

summary: A team of 22 athletes left the country for Hong Kong to compete in the Asian Junior (U20) Athletics Championship, scheduled to be held from May 28 to 31. All eyes will be on the 400m event, where two promising quarter-milers, Omel Silva and Sadew Rajaakaruna, are expected to shine. Both have recently recorded multiple sub-46 second performances. Sadew recently broke the junior national record previously held by former Asian Junior 400m gold medalist Aruna Darshana, clocking an impressive 45.53 seconds. Omel, meanwhile, boasts a personal best of 45.79 seconds—the same time with which Darshana won the gold medal at the 2018 championship.

title: Tuskers clinch historic CASA Sevens double
summary: The Sri Lanka men’s and women’s rugby sevens teams produced a stunning double victory to become the inaugural champions of the Central Asia and South Asia (CASA) Sevens Tournament in Uzbekistan last weekend. Led by skipper Srinath Sooriyabandara, the Sri Lanka men completed the tournament unbeaten and crushed India 31-10 in the final after already defeating the same opponents 33-12 in the preliminary round. At the same time, the Sri Lanka women, captained by Charani Liyanage, outclassed Kazakhstan 27-0 in a one-sided final to seal a memorable championship victory. The tournament featured six men’s and six women’s teams. Sri Lanka, India, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Mongolia fielded both men’s and women’s teams, while Pakistan competed only in the men’s category and Kazakhstan took part in the women’s event. Men’s squad included Srinath Sooriyabandara (captain), Janindu Dilshan (vice captain), Chathura Vidanalage, Akash Madusanka, Kavindu de Costa, Kavindu Perera, Ramith Himasha, Ravindu Anjula, Suranga Tennakoon, Diluksha Dange, Gayan Perera and Chemod Muthunayake, while Denuwan Wickramarachchi, Maliksha Perera and Jayathu Rajarathna were named as reserves. title: British School athletes shine in Thailand
summary: The British School in Colombo (BSC) emerged athletic champions at the FOBISIA Under-11 Primary Games held at the Pattana Sports Resort in Chonburi, Thailand. The FOBISIA Games have a long-standing reputation for being the most popular events in the FOBISIA calendar that offer students a fantastic opportunity to compete at the highest levels. Competing alongside seven other international schools in the Pink Group, the BSC students embraced every challenge, every event and every moment with energy and excitement to emerge athletics champions for 2026. In the swimming championship, BSC were placed fourth (just four points shy of third); the Teeball ‘A’ team finished fifth; Teeball ‘B’ team came fourth; Girls’ Football Team secured fourth place; and the Boys’ Football Team finished in fifth place. What stood out most was the sportsmanship the BSC students displayed both on and off the field. They competed with passion, respected opponents, celebrated others’ successes and represented BSC with pride, humility and kindness throughout the tour.

title: Ayatollah Khamenei’s iron grip on power in Iran comes to an end
summary: Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has been killed on the first day of massive US and Israeli air strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump has announced. The death of the 86-year-old ruler of the past three decades – one of the longest in the world – was later confirmed on Iranian State TV. Iran has had only two supreme leaders since the 1979 Islamic Revolution. It’s an all-powerful office – the supreme leader is Head of State and commander-in-chief of the armed forces, including the elite Revolutionary Guards. Khamenei is not quite a dictator, positioned in the middle of a complex web of competing power centres, able to veto any matter of public policy and hand pick candidates for public office. Young Iranians have never experienced life without him in charge. State television has covered Khamenei’s every move. His image is plastered on billboards in public spaces and his photograph is ubiquitous in shops. Abroad, successive Iranian presidents have often hogged the limelight. summary: Pakistan has bombed Afghanistan’s capital Kabul and other cities as fighting spread following attacks by Afghan forces against Pakistani military positions along their shared border earlier. Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Friday that his country’s “patience has run out” with the Taliban authorities in neighbouring Afghanistan, and that Pakistan would now be waging “open war”. Afghan anti-aircraft guns opened fire after the first raid and continued firing after the second, according to Shadid. summary: School holidays are precious, protected time for the Prince and Princess of Wales. Last week was half term. Prince William was back from his official visit to Saudi Arabia. title: UK comic Russell Brand pleads not guilty to new rape, sex assault charges
summary: British comedian and actor Russell Brand ⁠has pleaded not guilty to two further charges of rape and sexual assault nearly ⁠two decades ago. Brand appeared at Southwark Crown ⁠Court in London on Tuesday and denied accusations of raping one woman and sexually assaulting a second woman in 2009. Once one of the United Kingdom’s most high-profile broadcasters, he was charged last year with two counts of rape, one count of indecent assault and two ‌counts of sexual assault against four women between 1999 and 2005. Brand pleaded not guilty in May last year to those five charges and is due to stand trial in June. A hearing will be held next month to decide whether the new allegations should be joined to that case, with Brand’s lawyer ⁠saying his client needs more time to address ⁠the latest offences. “These new charges are in relation to two further women and are in addition to the charges issued to Brand in April 2025, which involved four women,” London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement in December. Brand, 50, arrived at court wearing a white cowboy hat and sunglasses. Asked how he was feeling, the actor, who said in 2024 he had become ⁠a Christian, told reporters he was feeling “blessed”. Born in 1975 to working-class parents in Essex, east of London, Brand began his stand-up career as a teenager, eventually working as an MTV presenter and host of a reality TV series. A regular on British screens in the ⁠2000s, he was known for his flamboyant ⁠style and appearance. He also worked as a radio presenter for the BBC. Brand starred in several films, includingGet Him to the Greekin 2010, the year he married American pop star Katy Perry. They divorced in 2012 after 14 months of marriage. By the early 2020s, Brand had faded from and has since largely appeared online, airing his views on US politics and free speech. (Al-Jazeera)

title: India cuts dividend tax for large French investors
summary: India and France have revised a three-decade-old tax treaty, reducing dividend levies for large French investors while expanding Delhi’s powers to tax some transactions. The changes could benefit major companies such as Sanofi, Renault and L’Oreal, which have expanded their investments in India over the past few years. The agreement also gives Delhi the right to tax capital gains arising from the sale of shares, including transactions where a French entity owns less than 10% of an Indian company. The revised treaty also removes a most-favoured-nation (MFN) clause which had allowed French entities to claim a lower tax rate in India. It will come into effect after completing formalities and legal approvals in both countries. During the visit, the countries announced the elevation of their relationship to a “Special Global Strategic Partnership” and deepened cooperation in areas such as defence and space technology. In a joint statement on 17 February, they welcomed the amendment to the bilateral tax treaty. They said it would “secure economic activity for French and Indian businesses and pave the way for greater investments and collaborations between the two countries”. title: Violence erupts in Mexico after drug lord El Mencho killed
summary: A wave of violence has broken out in Mexico after the country’s most wanted drug baron was killed in an operation seeking his arrest. Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “El Mencho”, was the leader of the feared Jalisco New Generation (CJNG) drug cartel and died after being seriously injured in clashes between his supporters and the Army on Sunday. Four CJNG members were killed during the operation in the town of Tapalpa, in the central-western Jalisco state, and three Army personnel were also injured, the Mexican Defence Ministry said. Retaliation for the drug lord’s death has seen violence spread to at least a dozen states, with CJNG blocking roads with burning vehicles. Throughout Sunday there were reports of gunmen on the streets in Jalisco and elsewhere. Eyewitnesses filmed plumes of smoke rising over several cities including Guadalajara – one of the host cities of the forthcoming Fifa World Cup. Jalisco’s Governor Pablo Lemus Navarro declared a code red in the state, pausing all public transport and cancelling mass events and in-person classes. Tourists who spoke to news agency Reuters described the resort town of Puerto Vallarta as a “war zone”. Some 250 roadblocks were in place across the country during the unrest, with 65 in Jalisco, the BBC’s US news partner CBS reported. In its latest update, the Mexican Security Cabinet said four blockades remained active in Jalisco. The Cabinet says 25 people have been arrested, 11 for their alleged participation in violent acts and 14 more for alleged looting and pillaging. title: Why Southasian diasporas are rejecting far-right politics
summary: By Inderjeet Parmar With 2026 already underway, the Southasian diaspora in the United States and United Kingdom stands at a pivotal crossroads. Rising far-right populism, economic anxieties, imperial overreach, and resurgent racism have placed these communities, once again, under intense pressure. Yet, far from succumbing to division or despair, the diaspora is increasingly contributing to broad, multiracial coalitions resisting authoritarianism, oligarchic capture, and elite dominance. The old chant “The people united will never be defeated”, resonates deeply. History repeatedly proves that when ordinary people overcome fear and manufactured divisions to stand together for justice and dignity, even the most entrenched powers falter. For Southasians in the U.S. and U.K., 2026 offers real prospects for hope, rooted in cross-community solidarity, anti-racist mobilisation, and a shared rejection of big-money rule. In the United States, the Southasian diaspora of over five million has faced a sharp escalation in hostility under Donald Trump’s second term. Hate incidents surged after the 2024 election – racial slurs increased by 66% while threats of violence went up by almost 60%, mostly against Southasians, according to the Stop AAPI Hate organisation. title: US shoots down Iranian drone approaching aircraft carrier, official says
summary: The U.S. military on Tuesday shot down an Iranian drone that “aggressively” approached the Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier in the Arabian Sea, the U.S. military said. The incident came as diplomats sought to arrange nuclear talks between Iran and the United States, and U.S. President Donald Trump warned that with U.S. warships heading toward Iran, “bad things” would probably happen if a deal could not be reached. Oil futures prices rose more than $1 per barrel after news the drone was shot down. The Iranian Shahed-139 drone was flying toward the carrier “with unclear intent” and was shot down by an F-35 U.S. fighter jet, the U.S. military said. “An F-35C fighter jet from Abraham Lincoln shot down the Iranian drone in self-defense and to protect the aircraft carrier and personnel on board,” said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson at the U.S. military’s Central Command. Iran’s U.N. mission declined to comment. Iran’s Tasnim news agency said connection had been lost with a drone in international waters, but the reason was unknown. No American service members were harmed during the incident and no U.S. equipment was damaged, he added. The Lincoln carrier strike group is the most visible part of a U.S. military buildup in the Middle East following a violent crackdown against anti-government demonstrations last month, the deadliest domestic unrest in Iran since its 1979 revolution. Trump, who stopped short of carrying out threats to intervene during the crackdown, has since demanded Tehran make nuclear concessions and sent a flotilla to its coast. He said last week Iran was “seriously talking,” while Tehran’s top security official, Ali Larijani, said arrangements for negotiations were under way. (Reuters)

title: Unable or Unwilling? Indonesia’s Failed Natural Disaster Response
summary: By Adelina Kamal and John Bryant The floods and landslides that swept northern parts of Sumatra, Indonesia’s westernmost major island, at the end of November and persisted into December claimed more than 1,200 lives, and more than a hundred are still missing. They also displaced over a million people at the peak of the crisis, and devastated communities across multiple provinces. Entire villages disappeared or were submerged under mud and industrial debris, critical infrastructure collapsed, and livelihoods were wiped out. This was less the result of an isolated disaster than the cumulative consequence of long-term ecological destruction, disaster governance failures, and extractive development policies that have progressively stripped away natural protective systems and exposed communities to foreseeable risks. For many Indonesians concerned at the slow pace of the Government’s response, the debate has centred on whether the Sumatra floods should have been declared a national disaster, given the central government’s reluctance to do so. But, this issue also touches on a more fundamental question: whether the Indonesian Government is unable – or unwilling to protect its people amid the ongoing ecological destruction in Sumatra. A State can be considered unable when the scale of a disaster exceeds its capacity, and the State responds in good faith by mobilising all available resources, including seeking, accepting, or welcoming international assistance. title: Bitcoin nears $100,000 as investors bet on crypto-friendly Trump policies
summary: Bitcoin is nearing the $100,000 mark as crypto enthusiasts bet that United States President-elect Donald Trump will usher in a more welcoming regulatory environment for digital assets. The world’s most popular digital currency rose as high as $99,073 on Thursday, extending its surge since Trump’s re-election on November 5. The commodity has risen more than 60 percent since election day as investors anticipate Trump’s incoming administration to ease regulatory and legal hurdles to its use. Trump, who called the asset a “scam” during his first term, accepted campaign donations in cryptocurrency, and has pledged to make the US “the crypto capital of the planet” and accumulate a national bitcoin reserve. Trump and his three sons in September also announced the launch of their own crypto business, World Liberty Financial, which investors have taken as a promising sign of the president-elect’s belief in the sector. In another bullish signal for the sector on Thursday, United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chair, Gary Gensler, who was widely disliked among crypto investors for his aggressive enforcement actions targeting the sector, confirmed that he would step down in January. Trump had pledged to fire Gensler on “day one” of his administration, though the president does not have the authority to remove the SEC chair before the end of his or her term. While viewed by supporters as a ticket to big returns and financial freedom, Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies are known for their volatility and have faced government crackdowns in several parts of the world. After climbing to a record high of $69,000 in late 2021, Bitcoin plunged to less than $16,000 over the following year. The commodity burst past its previous peak in March after gaining more than 300 percent since November 2022.

title: Universal Merit Awards 2024 will be held at BMICH, Colombo: Mahinda Rajapaksa will be the chief guest, Bollywood director Dushyant will direct
summary: India’s Allso Group is organizing the Universal Merit Awards 2024 at the BMICH International Convention Center in Colombo, the capital of Sri Lanka, on 7 August 2024. The director of the event is famous Bollywood film director Dushyant Pratap Singh. Prof Kartik Rawal, Chief Promoter of Universal Merit Awards, said that in the above program, former President and Prime Minister of Sri Lanka Mr. Mahinda Rajapaksa will be the chief guest and Deputy Speaker of Sri Lanka Parliament Ajit Rajapaksa will be the special guest. Franchise Batao founder and director Ashish Kumar Aggarwal is playing the role of executive producer in this program, while Astrologer Praveen Kumar Joshi is associated with this program as co-organizer. Director Dushyant Pratap Singh informed that talents from 12 countries are being included in this program, out of which selected personalities will be honored. He told that Sri Lanka’s famous music composer and singer Priyanath Rathnayak and chairman of Star Quest company Dr. Isuru Bandara is handling the local command of the program in Sri Lanka. Chief Promoter Prof Kartik Rawal told that his company Allso Group is organizing Universal Merit Awards 2024 in Colombo, Sri Lanka. For the award, he has given the responsibility of direction to famous Bollywood director Dushyant Pratap Singh. That is why he is sure because Dushyant has successfully completed such international programs before this. Director Dushyant Pratap Singh expressed his gratitude and said that apart from famous personalities of the film world of many countries, people associated with many social, cultural, teachers and other institutions from Sri Lanka and India will participate in this program and this program will achieve new heights.
